 Is a kit cheaper than the station and panels bought separately?
 Most of the time, yes, and the gap is large enough to check before you buy. Of the 32 kits with a current price for every part, 31 cost less than the station and panels bought one by one. The largest gap is $996 on the EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra + 4 x 400W Solar Panel. One kit costs more than its parts: the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max + 400W Solar Panel, by $401.
 The five biggest savings and the kits that cost the same or more. Kit price compared with the station and panel prices at the same store, checked Oct 30, 2026 or later. 31 of 32 kits cost less than their parts. 
 Each card shows two different comparisons, and they answer different questions. The struck-through price is the store’s own “compare at” figure, the number its sale is measured against. Our “parts separately” figure adds up today’s price of the same station and the same panels at the same store, so it tells you what the bundle saves right now.
 The two can disagree. When the station alone is on sale and the kit is not, the kit can cost more than the same parts bought separately. That is why we compare against the parts and not against the list price.
 Count the price without a tax credit. The IRS states that the 25D residential clean energy credit is not available for property placed in service after December 31, 2025, so a kit bought now gets no federal credit. Our guide to what a solar generator costs has the details.
 What you get in a power station with solar panel kit
 Every kit on this page pairs one station with panels from the same brand, but check the included cable or adapter before you connect them. Four numbers decide how well the pair works together, and the diagram follows one kit through them.
 Specs from Jackery. The 0.75 factor is our planning assumption, explained below. 
 Panel watts are measured in lab conditions. Outdoors we plan with 75% of them.
 Solar input is the most panel power the station accepts at once. Watts above it go unused in full sun.
 Voltage range sets which panels fit and how many you can wire in series. The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 , for example, takes 11 to 60V on its two 8mm DC ports and 400W in total.
 Capacity is what the battery holds. Divided by the watts that reach it, 75% of the panel rating capped at the station’s solar input, it gives the refill time on every card.
 How long does a kit take to refill the station?
 Divide the station’s capacity by the watts the panels deliver. We count 75% of the rated panel watts and cap the result at the station’s solar input limit. That share sits close to lab results: OutdoorGearLab measured 12 portable panels in July 2026 and got 56% to 91% of their rated watts. For the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 with one 200W panel, that is 1,070Wh ÷ 150W, or about 7 hours of full sun from empty.
 Full sun is not the same as daylight. Peak sun hours count how many hours a day the sun delivers its full strength, and they depend on where you live and the season. At 5 peak sun hours, the same kit collects 150W × 5 = 750Wh a day, so a full refill from empty takes about a day and a half. The solar charging calculator sets the peak sun hours for your ZIP code and turns the hours on each card into days.
 Some kits pair a panel rated above the station’s limit. The Explorer 2000 v2 accepts 400W of solar, and one of its kits comes with the 500W SolarSaga 500 X. At our 75% figure the panel gives about 375W, which is still under the limit. In weak light, such as morning or clouds, the extra rated watts can help, as long as voltage and current stay inside the station’s limits.
 Our planning figure: 75% 
 Heat, dust, wiring and a less than perfect angle cost about a quarter of a panel’s rated watts, so we multiply by 0.75. It is an assumption, not a measured efficiency, and our solar charging calculator uses the same figure.
 Can you use another brand's solar panel?
 Yes, if the panel fits the station’s solar input. Four limits decide it: the voltage range, the current, the maximum solar watts and the plug. The panels’ open-circuit voltage (Voc, printed on the label) has to stay inside the voltage range, and below the maximum even on a cold morning, when Voc rises. Panels wired in series add their Voc together. Jackery lists its SolarSaga 200W at 22V Voc, so two in series give about 44V and fit the 12 to 60V input of the Explorer 1000 v2. Three would reach about 66V and go over it.
 If a panel ends in MC4 plugs, an adapter cable from MC4 to the station’s port connects it. BLUETTI, for example, sells a 20A MC4 to XT60 cable for the Elite 100 V2. Panel watts above the station’s limit do not charge it any faster. The solar charging calculator runs the series check for your panel.  Camping and road trips: the lightest station among kits with at least 1,000Wh. That covers about two days of a 12V camping fridge plus phones, since Dometic lists its CFX3 35 at about 282Wh a day on 12V, and we plan with about 300Wh.
 Lowest price per Wh: the kit price divided by the station’s capacity, with the panels included in the price.

 Solar generator kits for camping
 On a camping trip, weight and daily solar output matter more than raw capacity. A kit that puts back what you use each sunny day lets you stay out without a hookup. Take a 12V fridge at about 300Wh a day plus phones and lights: one 200W panel collects about 750Wh on a day with 5 peak sun hours (200W × 0.75 × 5), more than the fridge uses.
 Illustration made with Adobe Firefly. 
 A small solar generator in the 300Wh class, such as the Jackery Explorer 300 v2 with a 40W panel, keeps phones, lights and a camera charged. It will not carry a fridge through a full day, because 288Wh at our 85% usable figure is about 245Wh. Our ranking of the best portable power station for camping compares the stations themselves, with and without panels.
 Questions buyers ask
 Does a solar generator come with solar panels? Not always. "Solar generator" is a brand name for a portable power station that can charge from the sun, and some listings sell it with panels and some without. Jackery's Solar Generator 1000 v2 page, for example, also offers the station alone, marked "solar panel not included". If you want a solar generator with panels, check that the variant you pick names the panel and its wattage.
 Can I use a third-party solar panel with my power station? Yes, if the numbers match. The panels' open-circuit voltage (Voc) must sit inside the station's input range, below the maximum even on a cold morning, the current must stay under the input limit, and the plug must fit the solar port, directly or through an adapter cable rated for that current. The station's solar input limit tells you how many panel watts are worth buying. The solar charging calculator runs the voltage check for series wiring. The table in the section on other brands' panels lists the voltage range and the plug of every station with a kit.
 Should I buy a kit now or add panels later? Buy the kit if the card shows a saving and you already know you will charge from the sun. Most kits we track cost less than the same parts bought one by one. Add panels later if you are not sure how much solar you need, or if the station alone is on sale. Each brand also sells its panels on their own, so you can match them to the station later.
 What does "with coupon" mean next to a kit price? Some stores, Anker SOLIX among them, show a coupon price on the product page. When the store lists a coupon as active today, we show the price after the coupon and mark it "with coupon". The coupon may need a code at checkout, so confirm the final price in the cart before you pay.

 A solar generator is not a fuel-burning machine. It is a portable power station: a rechargeable LiFePO4 battery, an inverter that turns stored DC into household AC, and a charge controller that accepts energy from folding solar panels. The panels refill the battery during daylight, and you draw from that stored energy at night or on cloudy days.
 That distinction matters for anyone shopping on a budget, because the number that decides how long your outage lasts is capacity in watt-hours, not the headline wattage on the box. A multi-layer BMS handles overcharge, over-discharge, overload, short circuit and overheating.
 What you can realistically run on it
 Toolboxes, laptops, televisions, lighting and phone charging are all within reach of 1,000W of pure sine wave output. The compact 7.9 by 7.9 by 11.6 inch footprint helps in a small vehicle or a tight closet.
 If you are buying mostly for the panel and the feature set rather than for a long runtime, the kit delivers a lot for the money.
 Where it falls short
 The manufacturer does not publish the battery capacity, which makes runtime impossible to compare properly against anything else on this list. That single omission should push cautious buyers toward a competitor that states its watt-hours.
 The warranty runs 12 months, the shortest of the eight, against five years on most rivals and three years on the DaranEner. USB-C PD tops out at 60W rather than 100W, there are only two AC outlets, and 10 percent of reviews are one star.

 The Cubus 600L is the lightest of the eight complete kits at 13.67 lb, and it is the easiest to move when you need power somewhere other than where it is stored. Buyers use it for routers, televisions, phones, laptops, e-bike battery top-ups and small loads during outages.
 Its most interesting technical detail is the 100W MPPT solar input. MPPT is normally a feature of larger charge controllers, and having it here means cheaper, smaller third-party panels can be wired together in parallel to speed off-grid charging.
 Recharging comes in three forms: 100W MPPT solar, 130W AC wall and 120W car. Pass-through charging lets devices run while the station refills, and the seven-port layout includes three pure sine wave AC outlets, a 100W PD USB-C, two 18W USB-A ports and a 120W car socket.
 The battery is LiFePO4 rated at 3,000-plus cycles to 80 percent with a stated 10-year design life, and the warranty is three years with 24/7 support. Owners frequently mention units being replaced without a return, which is the strongest service story we found at this budget.
 What you can realistically run on it
 Networking, televisions, phone charging, a laptop and lighting all sit comfortably within 576Wh. The 100W USB-C PD port charges a laptop at a reasonable speed, which is more than many competing compact kits offer.
 It is a sensible choice for an apartment, a travel vehicle or a home office where the goal is keeping the internet and communications alive rather than running a household.
 Where it falls short
 Continuous output is 600W, even though the listing headline pushes 1,200W peak. Treat the peak figure as a startup allowance, not a rating, and expect a coffee maker or microwave to be out of reach.
 At 576Wh it is one of the two smallest batteries in the roundup. Some owners report units shutting off during USB-C PD charging once the return window closed, the battery gauge does not always match true remaining capacity, and car charging cables are not included. Units can also arrive fully discharged, which is worth conditioning before first use.

 Bundle or Standalone: Does the Kit Include a Solar Panel?
 Ask this question before anything else. The most repeated complaint across prepper and off-grid forums for this exact query is buying a listing advertised as a solar generator and discovering the panel is a separate purchase, which pushes the real total over the ceiling you set.
 Every kit in this roundup includes a panel, but they are not equal. Three bundles here ship 200W or 220W panels, one ships 160W, and two ship only 100W. Panel size is the biggest driver of how quickly the station refills off-grid, and it is not visible in the headline wattage of the power station.
 Two details catch people out. Most of these bundles deliver the station and the panel in separate boxes, so plan for that when you are counting on getting power running in a hurry. And the station’s solar input ceiling is a separate number from the panel wattage, which matters if you plan to add panels later.
 Our advice is to buy the kit if you are buying for blackout backup where the wall outlet is your primary recharge path. Buy standalone only if you already own panels you like, since a station on its own is often not enough to keep a home running through a long outage.
 What a Sub-1000 Power Station Can Actually Run
 Runtime comes from one formula: watt-hours divided by watts gives hours. A 1,024Wh station running a 150W load gives roughly 6.8 hours before losses, and a 499Wh station running the same load gives about 3.3 hours. Everything else on this list follows from that arithmetic.
 Refrigerators are the case people ask about most. A typical fridge draws 100W to 300W while running with a startup surge well above that, so a 1,000Wh unit gives roughly 3 to 8 hours of continuous compressor time, or one to two days of duty-cycled operation. One owner on the Jackery reports nine hours on a full-size side-by-side.
 Networking is the easiest win. A router and a modem together pull 15W to 25W, which means a 500Wh unit runs a network for well over a day, and UPS mode keeps them alive without a visible interruption.
 Lighting, phone charging and laptops barely dent any of these banks. A 65W laptop charger running for four hours consumes about 260Wh, so even the smallest kit in this roundup handles several hours of remote work.
 Where expectations need adjusting: a space heater at 1,500W, a portable air conditioner, a microwave and a 1,000W coffee maker will each empty a 1kWh station in under an hour of continuous use. Heating and cooling are the loads that push you into a larger, more expensive machine.
 Power tools fall in the middle. A circular saw or a heat gun will run for a meaningful session on any of the 1kWh-class kits here, and the 4,500W surge on the OUPES Mega 1 and the 3,600W surge on the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic cover startup spikes comfortably.
 Medical equipment is its own category and worth reading the dedicated section below before you buy anything.
 Solar Panel Reality Check: Nameplate vs Real Output
 A 400W panel will run a fridge, but slowly. In good conditions a 400W panel realistically delivers 200W to 300W, which is enough to offset a refrigerator’s average draw on a sunny day and nowhere near enough to refill a 1kWh bank quickly.
 Expect the numbers to be lower than the label in several ways. Heat cuts output, angle and shading cost more, and a panel that is nominally 200W may deliver 125W to 145W in average measured conditions. Budget for roughly half to three-quarters of nameplate as a working estimate.
 That reframes what a panel is for. Included panels at this budget are an emergency top-up and a way to keep a station alive over a multi-day outage, not a replacement for wall charging. The 200W panel in the Anker, BLUETTI, Jackery and GRECELL bundles restores a 1kWh bank in roughly 6 to 7 hours of strong sun.
 The EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic is the outlier here. Its 220W bifacial panel produces around 190W to 200W in partial sun and recharges the station in about 5.8 hours, which is why it is the pick if you will genuinely be off-grid.
 Before buying a second panel, check the station’s solar input ceiling and its maximum current. The Delta 3 Classic accepts 500W at 15A maximum, so a low-voltage array cannot hit that ceiling, and the BLUETTI’s 1,000W ceiling gives you the most room to add panels later.
 How Long a 1000Wh Station Lasts in a Blackout?
 A typical household keeping the essentials running draws 200W to 600W in aggregate, which is the number worth planning against. On a 1,024Wh bank that is roughly 1.7 to 5 hours.
 The strategy that works is prioritization rather than endurance. Run the refrigerator, one lamp, the router and phone charging continuously, and switch everything else off. Reviewers who report multi-day coverage are almost all doing exactly that.
 Cycling matters too. A fridge that draws 150W on average across an hour has a very different profile from a load that pulls 150W continuously, so a duty-cycled appliance extends your window far more than the nameplate suggests.
 Be honest about the limit. Two weeks without electricity, which is the scenario forum users most often describe, is beyond what any sub-1,000 station can cover for a household. These units buy you a night or two of normal life with a refrigerator running, not a long-term replacement for grid power.
 For longer outages, the right move is to add capacity. The OUPES Mega 1 expands to 5,120Wh with two extra batteries, and our guide to solar generators for winter power outages covers the larger formats built for multi-day events.
 Jackery vs EcoFlow vs Anker SOLIX vs BLUETTI
 If you want one brand answer, Anker SOLIX and BLUETTI are the two that come out strongest in the sub-1,000 tier. Anker wins on recharge speed and owner volume. BLUETTI wins on solar input headroom and pass-through behavior.
 Anker’s strength is speed and polish. A 43-minute 0-80 percent recharge, an IP68 station and a 4.7 rating across more than 2,100 reviews is a mature product, and the app-based recharge control is more granular than most rivals.
 BLUETTI’s strength is openness. A 1,000W solar input ceiling, XT-60 connectors and true pass-through charging make it the easiest kit to pair with panels and equipment you already own, and prepper communities name BLUETTI most often as the trusted brand in this class.
 EcoFlow wins on app depth and panel options. The Delta 3 Classic pairs the deepest software here with the largest bundled panel, and the River 2 Max is the lowest-cost complete kit in the roundup.
 Jackery wins on portability and recognition. The lightest full-size unit at 23.8 lb with the strongest reported refrigerator runtime, though it costs the most of the eight and its charging headline needs context.
 For camping and RV use specifically, our guides to the best solar generators for camping and best portable solar generators for RV camping go deeper on weight, port layouts and low-draw setups.
 Medical Devices, UPS Mode and Safe Indoor Use
 Powered medical equipment is the most upvoted concern in the forums covering this topic, and it deserves a straight answer. Yes, these units can run a CPAP machine or an oxygen concentrator, but only with preparation.
 Check three things. Pure sine wave output protects sensitive electronics, and every kit in this roundup except the GRECELL specifies it. UPS switchover time determines whether your device notices the outage, and 10ms or less, which the BLUETTI, EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic and OUPES offer, is inside the tolerance of most CPAP machines and concentrators.
 Then test it. Run your actual machine on battery for a full night before you need it, watch for resets or error codes, and keep the unit within reach of the bed rather than in a garage. Forum users who report problems commonly skipped this step.
 On noise, there is nothing to worry about. These stations are silent, and the 30dB modes on the BLUETTI and Jackery are quiet enough to sleep beside, which is the opposite of a gas generator running in a hallway.
 Ventilation still matters. LiFePO4 chemistry has a low thermal runaway risk compared with older cells, but not zero, so keep the unit in a dry interior space away from direct sun and combustible materials rather than sealed in a hot closet.
 Who Should Spend More Than This Budget Tier
 Skip this tier if you need to heat or cool a room, run a well pump continuously, or carry power for more than about a week without a wall outlet. Each of those pushes you past 2kWh of storage and 3,000W of continuous output, which is a different category of machine.
 Skip it if your whole plan depends on solar only. As covered above, a 100W to 220W panel keeps a 1kWh station alive but does not refill it in a day, and multi-day off-grid living needs substantially more panel wattage than any of these bundles provide.
 Consider spending more if you want expansion later. Only the OUPES Mega 1 grows into a larger system, and the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic is specifically the version that does not expand, so buying it caps your ceiling at 1,024Wh.
 Stay at this tier if your goal is a refrigerator, lights, networking, device charging and a coffee maker during outages. That is exactly what a 1kWh-class kit was built for, and all eight of them here do it well.
 Battery Storage and Maintenance Advice
 Store the unit around 80 percent charge if it will sit unused. Leaving a battery at full for months accelerates degradation, and letting it sit below 20 percent does the same thing from the other direction.
 Unplug it once it is full, and expect to top it up every few months rather than leaving it connected indefinitely. Charge it fully before putting it away for winter, and bring it to a moderate temperature before using it in cold conditions, since lithium cells deliver noticeably less capacity when cold.
 If you are buying secondhand or several years down the road, check the cycle count in the app and confirm the displayed capacity still matches the nameplate figure. A station that has been cycled heavily will show a lower number, and that number tells you what you are actually buying.
 Finally, buy the largest capacity you can afford rather than the smallest. Cycle life is where these products succeed or fail over a decade, and more watt-hours means more usable energy for the same number of cycles.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best solar generator under 1,000 dollars?
 The Anker SOLIX C1000 paired with its 200W bifacial panel is the best solar generator under 1,000 dollars. It delivers 1,056Wh of LiFePO4 capacity, 1,800W of rated AC output, an 80 percent recharge in 43 minutes on AC and up to 600W of solar input. The BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 is the best value alternative, with true pass-through charging and a 1,000W solar input ceiling.
 Which brand of solar generator is the best?
 For the sub-1,000 dollar tier, Anker SOLIX leads on recharge speed and owner review volume, while BLUETTI leads on solar input headroom and pass-through charging. EcoFlow wins on app depth and bundled panel wattage, and Jackery wins on portability. All four use LiFePO4 cells and carry multi-year warranties.
 How long will a 1000 watt solar generator run a refrigerator?
 A typical refrigerator draws 100W to 300W while running, with a startup surge well above that. A 1,024Wh station gives roughly 3 to 8 hours of continuous compressor time, or one to two days of duty-cycled operation. One owner of the Jackery Solar Generator 1000 v2 reports about nine hours on a full-size side-by-side refrigerator.
 What can you run with a 1000 watt solar generator?
 Comfortably: a refrigerator, a router and modem, LED lighting, laptops, phone charging and televisions for several hours. Briefly: coffee makers, microwave ovens, power tools and heating or cooling equipment, which will each empty a 1kWh station in under an hour of continuous use. Continuous heating and air conditioning are outside what this budget tier can do.
 Does a solar generator under 1,000 dollars come with a solar panel?
 Not always, and this is the most common purchase mistake at this budget. Many listings advertise a power station only, leaving the panel as a separate purchase that pushes the true total over the ceiling. All eight kits in this roundup include a panel, though sizes range from 100W to 220W, and most deliver the station and panel in separate boxes.
 Can a solar generator run a CPAP or oxygen concentrator?
 Yes, provided the unit has pure sine wave output and a fast UPS switchover of 10ms or less, which covers most CPAP machines and oxygen concentrators. Test your specific device on battery for a full night before an emergency, keep the station close to where you sleep, and never leave it in a hot unventilated space.
 Will a 400W solar panel run a fridge?
 Yes, but slowly. A 400W panel realistically delivers 200W to 300W in good conditions, which offsets a refrigerator’s average draw on a sunny day but will not refill a 1kWh battery bank quickly. Expect roughly half to three-quarters of the nameplate wattage as a realistic working figure, and plan on wall charging for fast recovery.
 Final Verdict: Which Solar Generator Under 1000 Dollars Wins
 The Anker SOLIX C1000 with its 200W bifacial panel wins this roundup. It pairs 1,056Wh of LiFePO4 storage with 1,800W of rated output, a 43-minute recharge to 80 percent and a 600W solar input ceiling, and it carries the largest owner review base of the eight with a rating of 4.7.
 Buy the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 if pass-through charging and the highest solar input ceiling matter most to you. Buy the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic if you will be off-grid and the 220W panel is the deciding factor, and the OUPES Mega 1 if you need 2,000W of continuous output and room to expand to 5,120Wh later.
 For the best solar generators under 1000 dollars, there is no single winner for everyone, but there is a clear pattern: prioritize watt-hours over headline watts, confirm the panel is in the box, and treat surge and power-lifting figures as startup allowances rather than ratings.  Who should buy the DELTA 2 Max
 The DELTA 2 Max makes the most sense if you need more than 500W of solar input across its two inputs, or you already own compatible extra batteries. If future expansion is your main reason to buy, check battery stock first: the DELTA 2 Max Smart Extra Battery was sold out at the EcoFlow US store on October 24, 2026, and back in stock on October 27.
 The DELTA 3 Max has the same 2,048Wh and 2,400W at $899 member price, against $1,049 member price for the DELTA 2 Max (Oct 30, 2026). Check its stock before you compare.
 Three things to know before you buy:
 1,709 to 1,800Wh: the energy three testers got out of the AC outlets, 83% to 88% of the rated 2,048Wh.
 $0.51 per Wh: $1,049 member price for 2,048Wh on the EcoFlow US store (Oct 30, 2026).
 Expansion: up to 6,144Wh with two extra batteries. The DELTA 2 Max Smart Extra Battery was sold out on October 24, 2026, and back in stock on October 27.
 It suits home backup for a fridge, router and lights, RV trips and cabins where you plan to add batteries or more solar later. It is not suitable for 240V loads or a Smart Home Panel 2 installation. Compare its price per Wh with the DELTA 3 Max before you buy. Selected 120V household circuits need a compatible transfer setup confirmed by an electrician.
 Key specs of the US DELTA 2 Max
 The US DELTA 2 Max (model EFD350) has a 2,048Wh LiFePO4 battery and a 2,400W inverter. LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate) is a battery type that handles thousands of charge cycles. EcoFlow rates this one for 3,000 cycles before it drops to 80% of its capacity.

 Ports. It has 15 outputs: 6 AC outlets, 4 USB-A (two at 12W, two fast-charge at 18W), 2 USB-C at 100W each, a 12V car outlet and 2 DC5521 barrel ports. The car outlet and the two barrel ports share one 126W limit, so you cannot draw 126W from the car outlet and 38W from each barrel port at the same time.

 X-Boost. X-Boost lets some heaters and kettles rated up to 3,400W run by lowering the voltage. Compatible resistive appliances may run at reduced power and heat more slowly. X-Boost does not give 3,400W of normal continuous output, and EcoFlow does not guarantee it works with every appliance. For anything with a motor or electronics, plan with the normal 2,400W limit. X-Boost is not available in bypass mode, when the station runs AC loads while it charges from the wall. Do not plan a plugged-in setup around it.
 Weight. At 50 lb, think about how often and how far you will carry it, including stairs and the lift into a car.
 Cold. EcoFlow lists charging from 32 to 113°F and use from 14 to 113°F. At 25°F in a garage, use may stay within the published discharge range, but charging is outside the stated range. What works depends on the temperature of the battery pack itself and the station’s protection system. The manual does not mention a battery heater.
 What independent testers measured
 Three testers measured how much energy comes out of the AC outlets. They got between 1,709Wh and 1,800Wh, which is 83% to 88% of the rated 2,048Wh. The difference includes conversion losses, the station’s own power use and usable-energy limits. Each tester used a different load and method. These are the published results under different test conditions, not a validated performance range for every US unit.

 What this means for you:
 Plan with about 1,740Wh. That is 85% of 2,048Wh, the figure our calculators use, and it sits inside the test results.
 Low AC loads are less efficient. The station uses about 13.6W itself while the AC outlets are on (TheSolarLab). That overhead is small beside a 1,000W load and about a third of a 40W device’s draw. For devices that can run on DC, use the matching DC or USB port instead of AC.
 The cited reviewers reported full AC charging times from about 1.2 hours to 1 hour 50 minutes. The 1,800W rating is the top speed, not the speed for the whole charge. Digital Trends saw 1,590W.
 The 4,800W surge rating is not a promise. In the Digital Trends test, a miter saw tripped it once before it started on the next try. TheSolarLab reported trouble with loads above the 2,400W continuous rating in its tests. If you need it to start a fridge, pump or saw, test that exact device before you count on it.
 The UK and German results are from 230V versions. We show them next to the US result, not as US numbers.
 The dated tests are mostly from 2023. The battery and inverter specs are the same today, so the capacity numbers still help. Firmware updates since then may change app features and charging behavior.
 How long will the DELTA 2 Max run your appliances?
 At a 100W average AC load, such as a full-size fridge, our simplified calculation gives about 17 hours from a full charge. These are our calculations, not tests: 1,740Wh divided by the average draw of each device.

 Fridges and freezers. The average draw includes the time the compressor is off, so it is lower than the number you see while it runs. Room temperature, door openings and the thermostat all change it. A plug-in watt meter over a full day gives you a real number. Set the AC timeout to “Never” in the app, or the equivalent setting in your app version, so the station does not turn the AC off on its own. Our refrigerator watts guide has typical numbers.
 CPAP. Your machine, pressure and humidifier change the draw a lot. A DC adapter approved by your CPAP maker, plugged into the car outlet, avoids the AC inverter and may give a longer runtime. Test the full setup at home before a trip or a storm, and follow your doctor and CPAP maker on backup power. The CPAP battery calculator uses your own settings.

 DELTA 2 Max vs DELTA 3 Max and DELTA 3 Plus
 The DELTA 3 Max matches the DELTA 2 Max on capacity and output, at $899 member price against $1,049 member price (Oct 30, 2026). It takes half the solar input, and EcoFlow lists no extra battery for it. The DELTA 3 Plus has half the capacity and grows to about 5kWh.

 If it is available for less than the DELTA 2 Max, the DELTA 3 Max is the better value for buyers who charge mostly from the wall, do not need extra batteries and can live with four AC outlets. It weighs about 44.8 lb against 50 lb and switches to battery in under 10 ms. It has 4 AC outlets instead of 6 and one 500W solar input. Pick the DELTA 2 Max if you want more than 500W of solar or extra batteries later, and check that the battery is in stock first (see below). Our DELTA 2 Max vs DELTA 3 Max comparison goes through every spec.

 The DELTA 2 is the smaller model: 1,024Wh, 1,800W and 500W of solar on one input, at 27 lb. The DELTA 2 Max doubles the battery, adds 600W of output and a second solar input, at 50 lb. EcoFlow’s US store no longer has a DELTA 2 page. The 1,024Wh DELTA 2 Extra Battery does not work with the DELTA 2 Max. Compatibility is accessory-specific, and the similarly named batteries are not interchangeable in both directions.
 Other 2kWh options from BLUETTI and Anker
 Two other 2kWh options (Oct 30, 2026): the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 at $899, rated for 6,000+ cycles, and the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 at $899.99, rated for 4,000. Cycles are one factor. Compare solar input, extra batteries and the full system price too.
 Is the Extra Battery in stock, and what does a bigger system cost?
 The DELTA 2 Max takes up to two extra batteries. With two 2,048Wh DELTA 2 Max Smart Extra Batteries, you get 6,144Wh in total. EcoFlow also lists the older 2,016Wh DELTA Max Smart Extra Battery. With two of those, the total is 6,080Wh.
 Check stock before you buy the station. On October 24, 2026, EcoFlow’s US store marked the DELTA 2 Max Smart Extra Battery sold out, with a pre-order note. On October 27 it was back in stock.  The DELTA 2 Max has two solar inputs. Each input accepts 11 to 60V, up to 15A and up to 500W, for 1,000W combined. The DELTA 3 Max, for comparison, has one 500W input. EcoFlow says the full 1,000W charges it in about 2.3 hours.

 These are hours of strong, direct sun, not hours of daylight. A clear day gives only a few of them, so the 17 hours with one 160W panel means several days. Shade, clouds, panel angle and anything running from the station all add time.

 Choosing panels. EcoFlow lists up to two of its 400W panels or four of its 220W panels for this model. For third-party panels, check the complete string on each input. Its cold-weather open-circuit voltage (Voc) must stay below the station’s 60V limit. Also check operating voltage, current, polarity, connectors and the wiring against the station and panel documents. Each input is rated for 11 to 60V, 15A and up to 500W. Do not assume any two panels can share an input: verify the series or parallel setup before you connect them. Our solar charging calculator, in the Related tools links at the end of this page, estimates the time for your panels and location. On October 27, 2026, the EcoFlow US store had the DELTA 2 Max bundle with two 220W panels in stock.
 Can it back up a few home circuits?
 The DELTA 2 Max can back up a few chosen circuits at 120V only, through a manual transfer switch. It does not work with the Smart Home Panel 2, so it cannot run a 240V well pump or 240V central AC.
 Two options listed at the October 24 check:
 EcoFlow’s transfer switch page: a Reliance Pro Tran 2 with 6 circuits ($399) or 10 circuits ($499). The page names other DELTA models, not the DELTA 2 Max, so ask your electrician to confirm the cord and inlet. EcoFlow says a qualified electrician must install it.

 Safety rules for any power station:
 Never feed the house by plugging the station into a wall outlet (backfeeding). It puts utility line workers at risk and can start a fire.
 Connect to your panel only through a transfer switch or an interlock installed by a licensed electrician.
 On wall power. You can leave it plugged in and use it as backup. While it is on the wall, it passes wall power straight to your devices. The manual limits that to 15A, and to under 3 hours above 12A (about 1,440W at 120V). In an outage it switches to battery within 20 ms, according to the current online manual. The archived 2023 manual gave 30 ms. We have not timed the switch ourselves. EcoFlow says not to use it for servers or workstations that need a 0 ms switch.
 A fridge, a router and LED lights use a few hundred watts, well inside the 2,400W output. For a full plan, see our home battery backup guide .

 Step-by-step fixes for wall charging, solar charging, an EcoFlow reset and the warning icons are in the Related help links at the end of this page.
 Recall: we found no CPSC recall for the DELTA 2 Max. In October 2025, EcoFlow recalled about 25,030 units of the older DELTA Max 2000 (model EFD310) over a burn and fire risk. The DELTA 2 Max is model EFD350. Check the model number on your unit, not the name.
 Storage. For long-term storage, EcoFlow’s current online manual recommends fully charging the station, then discharging it to 60%, once every three months. It separately warns against leaving the device uncharged or unused for more than six months. Archived instructions differ, so follow the current guidance for your unit.
 Warranty: 5 years in the US. The full user manual is in the Sources list below.
 Should you wait for a sale? Price history
 The DELTA 2 Max sold for $1,029 on the EcoFlow US store from September 26 to October 14, 2026, and for $1,049 from October 15. The list price is $1,299.
 The lowest price we have recorded is $1,029, since tracking started on September 26, 2026. That is not an all-time low.
 Its strongest case is the two solar inputs or batteries you already own. If neither matters for your setup, compare its price with the DELTA 3 Max and the other 2kWh options above.
 EcoFlow also lists a refurbished DELTA 2 Max at $799. It was sold out on October 27, 2026. If it comes back, compare its warranty, not only the price.
 Current codes and sales are on our EcoFlow deals page .
 Illustrative purchase cost per delivered kWh
 If the battery reaches its rated 3,000 cycles, its purchase price works out to about $0.22 per kWh it delivers. This is a simplified allocation of the purchase price, not the total cost of stored electricity. It leaves out charging electricity, charging losses and aging over time, and assumes the battery reaches the stated cycle benchmark.
 The math:
 2.048kWh × 3,000 cycles = 6,144kWh

 Reaching 80% capacity is not the end of the battery’s usable life. This model covers the stated cycle rating, not all the energy the station may deliver over its lifetime. With occasional use, the battery is likely to age before it uses up its cycles. Our calculation does not model calendar aging and is not a forecast of service life. Try your own numbers in our battery cost per kWh calculator, linked in Related tools at the end of this page.

 DELTA 2 Max questions buyers ask
 How long will the EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max run a refrigerator?

 What’s the difference between the DELTA 2 and DELTA 2 Max?

The 1,024Wh DELTA 2 Extra Battery does not work with the DELTA 2 Max, so the similarly named batteries are not interchangeable in both directions.
 Is the DELTA 2 Max worth it?

 Can I leave my DELTA 2 Max plugged in all the time?
 Yes. On wall power it passes power through to your devices and switches to battery in an outage, within 20 ms according to the current online manual. In this bypass mode the US limit is 15A, and EcoFlow limits loads above 12A (about 1,440W) to under 3 hours. These limits are separate from the 2,400W battery inverter rating.  EcoFlow rates the battery for 3,000 cycles to 80% capacity. At one full cycle a day, that is about 8 years. That is a rating, not a promise: heat, cold, storage and age also wear the battery. The warranty is 5 years.

 Best Portable Power Stations for Camping
 By Victoria Boyanova · Updated Oct 16, 2026
 The best portable power station for camping is the lightest one that holds the energy your trip needs. For a weekend with a 12V cooler, the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 has the lowest current price among eligible models under 30 lb with a 12V car outlet and at least 783Wh rated, our calculated two-day screening threshold for a 300Wh-a-day cooler plan with a 20% allowance and 92% from 12V. It also has the highest listed solar-input ceiling among eligible models under 30 lb, 600W. For a short trip with phones and lights, the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus is the lightest eligible model at 10.4 lb. For nights below freezing, the BLUETTI Pioneer Na is the one eligible model under 50 lb that its maker rates for charging below 32°F. BLUETTI rates it to charge from 5°F, and to 60% at most below 14°F.
 We picked from the 31 models we track, not every station sold in the US, by weight, the 12V outlet, solar input and charging temperature. A model ranks only after its PowerSized review is published, and only while the configuration we price is in stock. On October 28, 2026, 21 of the 29 met both conditions. We used the brands' US specs, published tests and our own daily price data.

 How long will a 12V cooler run on a camping power station?
 In this guide, a 12V compressor cooler is the load that sizes the station. Dometic lists its CFX3 35 at 0.98Ah per hour at 12V, measured with 90°F outside and 39°F inside the cooler. That is about 282Wh a day (0.98Ah × 12V × 24 hours), and we plan with 300Wh. A hotter day, a colder setting or frequent lid openings can raise it, and milder weather can lower it. We use this cooler as an example, not a compatibility test.
 Running it from the station’s 12V outlet skips the AC inverter. We count 92% of rated capacity as delivered from the 12V outlet, a planning assumption, not a measured figure for every station. The cooler averages about 12W (282Wh ÷ 24 hours), a low load. At low loads the station’s own consumption takes a larger share, so these days are the least certain estimates on this page.

Phones, lights and a fan come out of the same battery, so subtract them first, or add them in the battery runtime calculator . The station’s own consumption also takes a share on a multi-day trip. If you use a measured delivered-energy result instead of our 92% assumption, do not subtract an assumed overhead separately when that result already includes it.
 Dometic rates the CFX3 35 at 7.5A on DC, about 90W (12V × 7.5A). The car outlets of all four picks are listed at 10A: the C1000 Gen 2 at 12V, 10A and 120W on Anker’s US product page, the Pioneer Na and the Explorer 2000 v2 at 12V and 10A, and the RIVER 3 Plus at 12.6V and 10A by StorageReview’s spec table. The listed 10A outlet rating is above the cooler’s 7.5A rated DC current. That comparison does not establish spare capacity for additional devices or verify compressor startup. Check shared-output limits, the cooler’s instructions and the supplied cable. Our suggestion: plug the cooler into the 12V outlet, not into an AC outlet through its power adapter, to skip the inverter step.
 Camping in cold weather: charging below freezing
 Most of the stations we track do not charge below freezing. In our database, 24 of the 29 models list 32°F as the lowest temperature for charging, and 2 list none. Our picks can still run below 32°F by their makers’ ratings: down to 14°F for the EcoFlow and Jackery picks, -4°F for the Anker pick and -13°F for the Pioneer Na.
 Our suggestions for a cold trip:
 Do not run a fuel-burning heater, stove or generator inside a tent, a camper or a closed car. Their exhaust carries carbon monoxide ( CPSC ).
 Keep the station in the car or the tent overnight, off the frozen ground. A tent or parked car can also drop below freezing, so check the station’s temperature reading before you charge.
 Charge it in the warmest part of the day, from the car or from panels, once the station is at or above the lowest charging temperature in its manual.
 Check the charging limits in the manual of your model before the trip.
 Three models in our database list charging below freezing: the BLUETTI Pioneer Na from 5°F, and the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus and the EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra from -4°F. The last two weigh 77.2 lb and 181.8 lb, over the 50 lb limit of our cold-weather rule. Even cold-rated cells give less in deep cold: BLUETTI rates the Pioneer Na at 80% of its capacity at -13°F.
 Charging from solar at a campsite
 Solar keeps a station going on a long trip, but panels and sun set the pace more than the station. At our planning figure of 75% of the panels’ rated watts reaching the solar input, a 200W panel in 4 equivalent peak-sun hours puts about 600Wh into the station’s solar input (200W × 0.75 × 4 hours). That is energy at the solar input, not energy delivered to the cooler. Charging losses, which our 75% figure does not count, and the 92% share from the 12V outlet bring it under the two days of our 300Wh cooler plan that 600Wh ÷ 300Wh suggests. Shade from trees, clouds and a low winter sun cut it further.
 Check three limits on the station’s solar input: watts, voltage and current. By our calculation, the C1000 Gen 2 can reach its listed 600W maximum only on the upper of its two input ranges, 29 to 60V, as its card explains. The Explorer 2000 v2 takes up to 400W through two 8mm inputs. The solar charging calculator works out the hours for your panels, and our solar generator picks and solar generator kits compare stations sold with panels.

 Noise at the campsite
 A power station has no engine. The sound comes from its cooling fans and inverter, and the fans run harder under heavy load and while charging fast. Makers list these figures, without saying at what distance they measured:
 EcoFlow lists the RIVER 3 Plus under 30 dB.
 Jackery lists the Explorer 2000 v2 at 30 dB in Quiet Mode and 45 dB at full load.
 Anker advertises “20dB Operation” for the C1000 Gen 2, but the cited page does not provide enough measurement conditions for a direct comparison. OutdoorGearLab reported loud fan noise near maximum output and did not expect the same issue with a single low-wattage load.
 Some campgrounds set hours for generators. In Yosemite, for example, generators may run only from 7 to 9 am, noon to 2 pm and 5 to 7 pm, and quiet hours are 10 pm to 6 am ( NPS , checked October 27, 2026). The rules name generators, so ask your campground how it treats a battery station, check its current rules before the trip and keep heavy loads for the daytime.
 If you bring a fuel generator, its exhaust carries carbon monoxide. The CPSC says to run one outside only, at least 20 feet from a home. Our suggestion: keep the same distance from tents, campers and vehicles.
 How much weight can you carry to camp?
 Weight decides whether a station leaves the car. Our picks run from 10.4 lb to 39.5 lb:

 Under 15 lb: the RIVER 3 Plus goes in one hand, with a day pack in the other.
 About 25 lb: the C1000 Gen 2 is a short carry with both hands, from the car to a site nearby.

 How we chose these picks
 We compared the 31 portable power stations in the PowerSized database, US versions only. It is the list of models we track, not every station sold in the US. A model is eligible when the configuration we price is in stock at the brand's US store and its price was checked in the last 72 hours. In stock means the store takes the order and ships it without a stated future date or a stated wait longer than about a week, so pre-orders and backorders do not count. On October 28, 2026, 21 of the 29 models were eligible. A model becomes eligible only after its PowerSized review is published, so our recommendation pool is narrower than all products recorded in the database. Each job has one rule, and one model can win more than one job:

Days and hours on this page are our calculations of energy, not tests, and include no allowance unless stated. A solar-input energy benchmark is rated capacity divided by 75% of the panels' rated watts, subject to the supported connection and applicable input limits, in equivalent peak-sun hours, not a measured recharge time. Calculations use unrounded values, and displayed figures are rounded. Where we add an allowance, it is 20% on the load energy.  Questions campers ask
 What is the best power station to take camping? The lightest one that holds the energy your trip needs. For phones and lights, the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus , the lightest eligible model at 10.4 lb. For a weekend with a 12V cooler, the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 , about 3.1 days of a 300Wh-a-day cooler by our calculation, with no allowance. For freezing nights, the BLUETTI Pioneer Na , rated by BLUETTI to charge from 5°F, and to 60% at most below 14°F.
 How big of a power station do I need for camping? Add up the watt-hours of a day: a 12V cooler at about 300Wh, plus phones, lights and anything else. Multiply by the days, add 20% and divide by 0.92 for 12V loads or 0.85 for AC loads. For a mixed setup, calculate the DC and AC energy requirements separately using the corresponding assumption, then add the rated-capacity estimates. Under our 92% DC-delivery assumption and 20% load-energy allowance, two 300Wh days give a calculated reference size of 783Wh rated (300Wh × 2 × 1.2 ÷ 0.92 = 782.6Wh, rounded up). This is not a validated minimum for every station and cooler combination. The size calculator checks your list.
 Is a power bank or a power station better for camping? A power bank charges phones and small USB devices. A 20,000mAh bank holds about 74Wh (20,000mAh × 3.7V ÷ 1,000), about a quarter of our 300Wh cooler day. A power station adds AC outlets and a 12V car outlet, so it can run a 12V cooler or a fan. For phones and a headlamp on a short trip, a power bank is often enough. For a 12V cooler, plan on a station.
 Can a portable power station run a heater while camping? Not for long. By our 85% figure, a 1,500W space heater uses up a 1,024Wh station in about 35 minutes (1,024Wh × 0.85 ÷ 1,500W × 60), or about 1.2 hours at 750W. For a 12V heated blanket, hours = rated Wh × 0.92 ÷ the watts on its label. Do not run a fuel-burning heater in a tent or a closed car: its exhaust carries carbon monoxide. For a CPAP, see our CPAP power guide .
 Is a power station quieter than a generator for camping? It has no engine. The sound comes from its fans and inverter, and the level varies. EcoFlow lists the RIVER 3 Plus under 30 dB without stating the load, and Jackery lists the Explorer 2000 v2 at 30 dB in Quiet Mode and 45 dB at full load. Neither says at what distance.  Can you charge a power station from your car while camping? Often yes, using the car charging cable and input connection specified by the station maker. Anker's C1000 Gen 2 guide supports car recharging and says the cable is sold separately. Do not confuse its 120W car-socket output rating with the charging input. Check the supported input, vehicle socket limit and cable before estimating charging time. Run the engine only outdoors, where idling is allowed.

 SHARE 
 Highlights
 TL;DR: A solar generator is a portable power station paired with solar panels, so it makes its own power instead of just storing it. Our top picks: the Jackery Solar Generator 2000 Plus Kit (best overall), the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 Solar Kit (best for whole-home backup), the BLUETTI AC200L + SP200L Kit (best value), the BLUETTI AC180 solar kit (best budget), and the Jackery Solar Generator 1000 v2 (best for camping). The spec that matters most: solar input watts, not just battery capacity.
 Power outages aren’t getting shorter. The average U.S. customer lost about  11 hours to power interruptions in 2024 , the U.S. Energy Information Administration reports, nearly double the yearly average from the decade before.
 A gas generator can bridge that gap. So can a solar generator, minus the fumes, the noise, and the trips to the gas station.
 But “solar generator” gets thrown around loosely. Plenty of listings use the term for a battery that’s never seen a solar panel. We only recommend kits here that actually pair a power station with real solar input, and we picked them based on how fast they recharge from the sun, not just how big the battery is.
 Our Top Picks at a Glance
 Pick Battery Capacity Solar Input Best For 
 Jackery Solar Generator 2000 Plus Kit 2,042Wh (expandable to 12kWh) Up to 400W Best overall 
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 Solar Kit 4,096Wh (expandable to 48kWh) Up to 2,600W Whole-home backup 
 BLUETTI AC200L + SP200L Kit 2,048Wh (expandable to 8,192Wh) Up to 1,200W Best value 
 BLUETTI AC180 Solar Kit 1,152Wh Up to 500W Best budget 
 Jackery Solar Generator 1000 v2 1,070Wh Up to 400W Camping and portability 
 What Is a Solar Generator, Exactly?
 A solar generator is a portable power station connected to one or more solar panels, so the battery recharges from sunlight instead of only a wall outlet.  EcoFlow’s own breakdown of the two categories  puts it simply: a power station stores energy, a solar generator actively makes it.
 That distinction matters more than marketing copy suggests. A power station without panels is just a big rechargeable battery. It’ll get you through an outage once, then it’s dead until you find an outlet.
 Add solar panels and the equation changes. As long as the sun’s out, you’re topping the battery back up. That’s the real value of a solar generator over a  gas generator : you’re not driving anywhere for fuel.
 Jackery’s guide to the difference between a solar generator, a power station, and a solar panel  makes the same point: if you buy a power station and solar panels separately, you’ve built a solar generator setup yourself. Buying a kit just bundles the two so you don’t have to match specs on your own.
 What Size Solar Generator Do You Need?
 Match the battery to what you actually plan to run, not the biggest number you can afford. A 1,000 to 2,000Wh battery covers phones, a router, some lights, and a mini fridge through a short outage. Anything bigger, especially a full-size fridge or a window AC unit, needs 2,000Wh or more.
 Two numbers decide what a solar generator can do for you: watt-hours (Wh) and watts (W). Watt-hours are the fuel tank, they tell you how long the battery lasts. Watts are the engine, they tell you what you can plug in at once without tripping the inverter.
 Running a full-size fridge at roughly 150W alongside internet and a few lights drains a 2,000Wh battery in about 10 to 20 hours. If you want to see exactly what your gear would pull from one of these, our breakdown of  what a portable power station can actually run  walks through real appliance math.
 Best Solar Generators of 2026
 These five kits cover the range from weekend camping to keeping the lights on through a multi-day outage. All of them ship with, or offer, real solar panels rated for meaningful input wattage, not a token 30W trickle charger.
 1. Jackery Solar Generator 2000 Plus Kit (Best Overall) 
 This kit pairs the Explorer 2000 Plus with two SolarSaga 200W panels. The battery starts at 2,042Wh and expands to 12kWh with add-on packs, which is enough headroom to grow from “backup for a few rooms” to “backup for most of the house” without replacing the unit. It handles up to 6,000W of combined output in parallel setups and takes solar input up to 400W across the two panels.
 Check on Amazon 
 2. EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 Solar Kit (Best for Whole-Home Backup) 
 The  DELTA Pro 3 so l ar kit  is built for people who want a real alternative to a whole-home generator. It holds 4,096Wh out of the box, expands to 48kWh, and outputs 4,000W (6,000W with X-Boost). Its solar input tops out at 2,600W across two MPPT ports, with 99% tracking efficiency, so it recharges faster from the sun than most home-backup units on the market.
 Check at ECOFLOW 
 Check on Amazon 
 3. BLUETTI AC200L + SP200L Kit (Best Value) 
 The  AC200L solar kit  lands in the middle of the pack on price for what it delivers: 2,048Wh of storage, 2,400W of output, and up to 1,200W of solar input. That input number is the story here. It’ll pull a full recharge from the sun in a fraction of the time a similarly sized unit with a 200W or 300W solar cap would need. It also expands to 8,192Wh if you outgrow the base unit.
 Check on Amazon 
 4. BLUETTI AC180 Solar Kit (Best Budget) 
 For readers who want real solar charging without the flagship price tag, the  AC180  pairs a 1,152Wh battery with up to 500W of solar input, which is generous for this size class. Add a 200W panel and you’re looking at a recharge window well under 10 hours in decent sun, according to BLUETTI’s own charging figures.
 Check on Amazon 
 5. Jackery Solar Generator 1000 v2 (Best for Camping and Portability) 
 The  Solar Generator 1000 v2 kit  is built around Jackery’s smaller Explorer 1000 v2, which weighs under 24 pounds and hits a 1-hour fast charge from AC power. It still takes up to 400W of solar input, so a couple of hours of good sun gets you most of the way back to full. If your use case leans more toward  camping trips than outages , this is the pick to start with.
 Check on Amazon 
 How Fast Do Solar Panels Actually Recharge These?
 Charging time from solar comes down to three things: panel wattage, hours of direct sun, and how efficient the built-in charge controller is. Most solar generators worth buying use MPPT (maximum power point tracking) controllers, which  pull up to 25% more usable power from the same panels than older PWM controllers .
 As a rough rule of thumb, aim for solar wattage that can refill your battery in 5 to 6 hours of peak sun. A 2,000Wh battery pairs well with 400 to 500W of panels. Undersize the panels and you’ll be waiting two or three days for a full charge instead of one afternoon.
 Cloud cover, panel angle, and time of year all cut into that number too. Treat manufacturer charge-time estimates as a best case, not a guarantee.
 Solar Generator vs. Gas Generator for Outages
 A solar generator wins on convenience and safety for most home backup needs. It produces no carbon monoxide, so it’s safe to run indoors, and it’s quiet enough to sit next to while you sleep. A gas generator needs to run outdoors, needs fuel you have to store and rotate, and needs maintenance to start reliably when you actually need it.
 Where gas still wins: raw output for whole-house loads like central air, and the ability to refuel instantly at 2 a.m. instead of waiting for daylight. If you’re weighing the two head to head, our full  solar generator vs. gas generator comparison breaks down the tradeoffs in more detail.
 For camping specifically, the calculus tilts even further toward solar. No fuel to haul, no fumes near the tent, and panels that do double duty charging phones and running a cooler during the day.
 Do You Need the Home Backup Size or the Portable Size?
 If your goal is keeping a fridge, router, and a few lights running through a multi-day outage, you want the 2,000Wh-plus tier, closer to the DELTA Pro 3 or AC200L in this list. Our full  home backup power station picks  go deeper on sizing a system for that use case specifically.
 If you mainly need something for weekend trips, tailgating, or a laptop and phone during a shorter outage, the smaller kits like the Jackery 1000 v2 or the AC180 make more sense. Don’t pay for capacity you won’t use. If budget is the deciding factor over sizing, our  power stations under $500  roundup covers the entry-level tier without solar bundled in, useful if you want to add panels separately later.
 Is a Solar Generator Worth It?
 For most homeowners in outage-prone areas, yes. The upfront cost is higher than a comparable gas generator, but there’s no ongoing fuel cost, no annual maintenance visit, and no carbon monoxide risk. Over a few years of outages, that gap narrows fast.
 The honest caveat: a solar generator won’t run central air or a well pump for days on end the way a whole-home gas or propane system can. It’s built for the “keep the essentials running comfortably” tier of backup, not total energy independence. For most households, that’s exactly the gap that needs filling.
 If you’re deciding between EcoFlow, Jackery, and BLUETTI specifically, our  EcoFlow vs. Jackery vs. BLUETTI comparison  breaks down how the three brands differ beyond just this list.
 Pick the size that matches what you actually need to run, check that the solar input watts match your panel setup, and you’ll have a system that earns its keep the next time the grid goes down.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can a solar generator power a whole house? 
 A large unit like the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 , especially when expanded with extra battery packs, can cover most essential circuits during an outage. It won’t run everything at once the way a whole-home standby generator does, but it can keep a fridge, lights, internet, and small appliances running for days.
 How long do solar generators last? 
 Most current models use LiFePO4 batteries, which are rated for thousands of charge cycles, often 3,000 to 4,500 depending on the brand, before capacity drops meaningfully. Used a few times a year for backup, that translates to well over a decade of useful life.
 Do I need special solar panels, or will any panel work? 
 You need a panel that matches your unit’s voltage and connector type, or you’ll need an adapter. Manufacturer-matched panels (Jackery SolarSaga, EcoFlow’s own panels, BLUETTI’s PV series) are the safest bet since they’re tuned for that unit’s MPPT controller and won’t need extra troubleshooting.
 Is a solar generator worth it over a gas generator? 
 For most homeowners dealing with occasional outages, yes. You skip the fuel storage, the noise, and the carbon monoxide risk, and you can run it indoors. Gas still wins if you need to power heavy whole-house loads like central air for extended periods.
 Can a solar generator charge on a cloudy day? 
 Yes, but slower. Solar panels still produce power in overcast conditions, typically 10 to 25% of their rated output, so a charge that takes 5 hours in full sun might take most of a day under heavy cloud cover.

FAQ

Can I buy the panel first?
Usually no. The station’s watt/Voc limits and connector decide the panel.

Do I need Amazon adapters if the brand cable is in the box?
No. Adapters are for spares, length, or a second-panel parallel run you already sized.

Is a “solar generator kit” on a marketplace the same thing?
Often a station + panel + cable with vague Voc claims. Prefer named models you can check against the station’s max PV voltage.

Apartment balcony only?
Station first; panel second and only if you have safe sun and building rules allow it. Start with apartment / condo blackouts.
